hints: Remember stereoisomers here means both E/Z isomerism at the C=C bond and optical isomerism at any chiral centre, so check for both.
For E/Z to exist, each carbon of the C=C bond must have two different groups, so quickly draw C2 and C3 for each alkene.
Now look for a carbon with four different groups attached, and combine the E/Z possibilities with the optical possibilities to find the total.
walkthrough:
**Recall the two types of stereoisomerism**

Great start. Alkenes can show cis-trans or E/Z isomerism, and molecules with a chiral centre can show optical isomerism.

Total stereoisomers = (number from E/Z) x (number from chirality)

**Check E/Z for the C=C at position 2**

For E/Z, each C of the double bond needs two different substituents.

For $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CH-}$, C2 has $\text{H}$ and $\text{CH}_3$, which are different, so E/Z is possible unless C3 fails.

**Test C3 in each option**

Look at the other end of the double bond, C3:

A $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{C=CH-}$: C2 has two $\text{CH}_3$ groups, so no E/Z.

B $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=C(CH}_3\text{)-}$: C3 has $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, so E/Z is possible.

C $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CH-CH(CH}_3\text{)-}$: C3 has $\text{H}$ and $\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, so E/Z is possible.

D $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CH-CH}_2\text{-}$: C3 has $\text{H}$ and $\text{CH}_2\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)}_2$, so E/Z is possible.

**Check for a chiral centre**

A chiral carbon has four different groups. Only one molecule has this.

In 4-methylhex-2-ene, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CH-}\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, C4 is bonded to $\text{H}$, $\text{CH}_3$, $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{CH=CHCH}_3$. All four are different, so C4 is chiral and gives a pair of enantiomers.

**Combine and conclude**

Option A has no E/Z and no chiral centre, so 1 form only.

Options B and D have E/Z (2 forms) but no chiral centre, so 2 stereoisomers.

The 4-methyl isomer has E/Z (2 forms) and a chiral centre (2 forms):
$$ \text{total} = 2 \times 2 = 4 $$
That is the greatest number.

options.A: Incorrect. 2-methylhex-2-ene is $(CH_3)_2C=CHCH_2CH_2CH_3$. C2 has two identical methyl groups, so E/Z isomerism is impossible, and there is no chiral centre. It has only 1 stereoisomer.
options.B: Incorrect. 3-methylhex-2-ene is $CH_3CH=C(CH_3)CH_2CH_2CH_3$. It does show E/Z isomerism (2 forms) because both C2 and C3 have two different groups, but C3 is $sp^2$ and no other carbon has four different groups, so there is no optical isomerism. Total is 2.
options.C: Correct. 4-methylhex-2-ene is $CH_3CH=CHCH(CH_3)CH_2CH_3$. It shows E/Z isomerism at C2=C3 (E and Z forms) and has a chiral centre at C4 with four different groups. Each geometric isomer exists as a pair of enantiomers, giving 2 x 2 = 4 stereoisomers, the most in the list.
options.D: Incorrect. 5-methylhex-2-ene is $CH_3CH=CHCH_2CH(CH_3)_2$. It shows E/Z isomerism (2 forms), but C5 is bonded to two $CH_3$ groups (C6 and the methyl branch), so it is not chiral. Total is only 2 stereoisomers.
